content: The aircraft emergency frequency, commonly referred to as guard, is a designated radio frequency within the aircraft radio band that is specifically reserved for emergency communications involving aircraft in distress. For military use, the frequency 243.0 MHz is employed, which is also known as Military Air Distress (MAD). Both the civilian and military emergency frequencies are utilized on an international scale. The frequency 121.5 MHz is actively monitored by most air traffic control towers, Flight Service Stations (FSS), national air traffic control centers, and other flight and emergency services. Separate frequencies are allocated for military and other government-related emergency communications. In the United Kingdom, 121.5 MHz is monitored by the Royal Air Force Distress and Diversion Cells (commonly referred to as D&D) located at the London Terminal Control Centre and the Scottish Oceanic and Area Control Centre. These centers operate through a nationwide network of antennas to ensure comprehensive coverage. In the event of an impact or emergency, the frequency 121.5 MHz is used for local homing purposes. Satellites are equipped to detect emergency signals transmitted on these frequencies and subsequently alert local personnel to the situation. This system enables search and rescue teams to locate the site of an accident more efficiently. Emergency beacons operating on 406 MHz are encoded with specific information, allowing the identification of the originating vessel. This encoding helps to quickly verify false alarms and ensures a more accurate response. The older 121.5 MHz-only beacons have been gradually phased out since early 2009 in favor of the more advanced 406 MHz beacons.
